questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes how the shared responsibility model actually behaves, as opposed to a fixed 50/50 split?
options: The responsibility line slides with the service model: IaaS leaves the guest OS and network configuration to the customer, PaaS moves OS/engine management to the provider while the customer still owns data, access, and service configuration, and SaaS pushes almost everything to the provider except identity and data
The split is always exactly 50/50 between provider and customer, regardless of whether the service is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS
The cloud provider is responsible for everything once data is stored in their cloud, including identity and data classification
The customer is responsible for the physical datacenter and host hardware on every service model
The responsibility line is identical for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS, since all three run on the same underlying infrastructure
questions.explain: The model isn't a fixed split — it's a line that slides along the stack depending on the service. An EC2 instance (IaaS) leaves the guest OS, patching, and network config to the customer; Azure SQL Database (PaaS) moves engine and OS management to the provider while the customer still owns data, access, and service configuration; Microsoft 365 (SaaS) pushes nearly everything to the provider except identity and data. Getting this wrong means either leaving a gap assuming 'the provider handles that' or duplicating controls the provider already owns.
questions.distractorExplain: Treating the split as a fixed 50/50 is exactly the misconception this lesson corrects — the real-world breaches it cites (Equifax, exposed S3 buckets) all happened on the customer's side of a line that had actually moved toward the provider for that specific service, not because the split was evenly divided.

questions.prompt: Match each Azure security primitive from Lesson 2 to its AWS equivalent.
left: Azure Monitor / Log Analytics / Activity Log
right: AWS Config rules + Service Control Policies (SCPs)
questions.explain: Lesson 2's table is meant to be read as a Rosetta Stone: Entra ID maps to AWS IAM plus IAM Identity Center for identity, Azure Policy maps to AWS Config rules plus SCPs for policy enforcement at scale, Defender for Cloud maps to Security Hub for posture management, and Azure Monitor/Activity Log maps to CloudTrail/CloudWatch for centralized logging — one underlying primitive, two vendor-specific implementations each time.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: CIS Benchmark recommendations are organized into Level 1 and Level ________ profiles, the second being stricter 'defense in depth' items adopted deliberately based on risk tolerance rather than by default.
questions.explain: Level 1 recommendations have minimal impact on performance or usability and nearly every organization implements all of them; Level 2 recommendations introduce real operational tradeoffs — more restrictive network rules, stricter key rotation — and are adopted deliberately where the tradeoff is justified, not as a default.

questions.prompt: Policy A requires MFA for a user; Policy B requires a compliant device for the same user. Both policies' assignments and conditions match the same sign-in attempt. Per Lesson 5, what does Entra ID actually require of that sign-in?
options: Both MFA and a compliant device — Entra ID evaluates every matching policy, and all of their grant controls must be satisfied, not just the strictest single policy
Only the compliant device requirement, since it's the stricter of the two
Only MFA, since Conditional Access always picks the single best-matching policy
Neither requirement, since two policies matching the same sign-in cancel each other out
questions.explain: Entra ID doesn't pick 'the best matching policy' — every policy whose assignments and conditions match gets evaluated, and all of their grant controls must be satisfied. If Policy A requires MFA and Policy B requires a compliant device for the same user, both apply: the user needs MFA AND a compliant device, even though no single policy said that. Designing policies assuming they'll stack with everything else in the tenant is exactly the discipline Lesson 5 teaches.

questions.prompt: An administrator is eligible, but not active, for the Global Administrator role in PIM. Per Lesson 6, what does 'eligible' actually mean here?
options: The admin can activate the role for a bounded time window when needed, but doesn't hold it continuously
The admin already holds the role permanently, identical to a classic standing assignment
The admin has no path to ever obtain the role without a separate approval process being created from scratch
Eligible and active mean the same thing in PIM, just different wording for the same state
questions.explain: PIM's entire model rests on the eligible/active distinction: eligible means a principal can activate a role for a limited, bounded window when they actually need it, while active means they hold it right now, exactly like a classic permanent assignment. The goal of a mature PIM configuration is almost nobody holding permanent active assignments to anything sensitive — instead holding eligible assignments activated just-in-time.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Policy effects, per Lesson 7.
options: Deny stops a non-compliant resource from being created or updated at all
Audit lets the write through but flags the resource non-compliant in the compliance dashboard
DeployIfNotExists can actively remediate by deploying a related resource, using a managed identity with its own scoped RBAC permissions
Azure Policy evaluates who the caller is, the exact same question Azure RBAC answers
An Azure Owner can never be blocked by a Policy effect, since RBAC already grants them unrestricted Actions
questions.explain: Deny blocks a non-compliant write outright, Audit lets it through while flagging non-compliance, and DeployIfNotExists actively remediates using a managed identity. Policy answers a genuinely different question than RBAC — 'is this resource's configuration allowed' rather than 'can this principal attempt this action' — which is exactly why an Owner can still be blocked from creating a non-compliant resource even though RBAC grants them unrestricted Actions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: of the three service principal credential types, ________ credentials let an external workload exchange its own OIDC token for an Entra ID token with no secret stored anywhere, making them the preferred option whenever the calling platform supports it.
questions.explain: Federated credentials (workload identity federation) let a GitHub Actions run, a Kubernetes pod, or another cloud's workload identity present an OIDC token and exchange it for an Entra ID token, with no secret stored anywhere, ever — the preferred option over certificates or client secrets whenever OIDC federation is supported.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes how AWS IAM evaluates multiple applicable policies for a single request?
options: An explicit Deny in any applicable policy always wins; otherwise the action is denied by default unless some policy explicitly allows it
The most permissive matching policy always wins, regardless of any explicit Deny elsewhere
IAM grants an implicit allow by default whenever no policy explicitly denies the action
An explicit Allow always overrides an explicit Deny, since Allow is the more specific statement
Policies are evaluated strictly in the order they were attached, and the first matching statement wins
questions.explain: IAM's evaluation logic is deterministic: an explicit Deny anywhere in any applicable policy wins, full stop, regardless of how many Allow statements also match. If nothing explicitly allows the action, it's denied by default — there is no implicit allow in IAM. That ordering is why a single well-placed Deny statement is powerful and a single overly broad Allow statement is dangerous.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes an implicit allow, which doesn't exist in IAM at all — the default state of every IAM principal, for every action, is denied until a policy explicitly allows it. Assuming silence means 'allowed' is exactly backwards from how IAM actually evaluates a request.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS Service Control Policies (SCPs), per Lesson 10.
options: An SCP can only ever take permissions away — it never grants one
The default FullAWSAccess SCP attached at the organization root adds no additional restriction until replaced or supplemented
A request only succeeds if both the identity-based IAM policy and every applicable SCP allow it
An SCP can grant a permission that no IAM policy in the account allows
SCPs replace the need to write any IAM policies inside member accounts
questions.explain: An SCP defines the ceiling on what IAM is even allowed to say yes to — it can restrict, but it can never grant. FullAWSAccess, the default root SCP, adds no restriction on its own. Because SCPs add another ceiling on top of ordinary IAM evaluation, a request only succeeds when both the IAM policy and every applicable SCP agree — an SCP cannot be the reason a request succeeds, and an actual grant still has to come from an IAM policy inside the account.

questions.prompt: Match each IAM term from Lesson 11 to what it actually is.
right: Short-lived access key, secret key, and session token issued by STS with a defined expiration
A persistent identity with credentials, like a password or access keys, that don't expire on their own
Defines who is allowed to assume a role — separate from what the role can actually do once assumed
An identity with no credentials of its own; principals assume it via sts:AssumeRole to get temporary credentials
questions.explain: An IAM user holds long-lived credentials that don't expire on their own. An IAM role has no credentials at all — it's assumed via sts:AssumeRole. A trust policy answers only 'who can assume this role,' a separate question from the permissions policy answering 'what can it do.' Temporary security credentials are what assuming a role actually hands back: a short-lived access key, secret key, and session token.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: IAM Access Analyzer calls the account or Organization it's scoped to the ________ of trust — access reaching a resource from outside it is exactly what generates a finding.
questions.explain: A zone of trust is either a single AWS account or an entire AWS Organization. Anything inside it is assumed trusted by default; anything outside — another account, a different Organization, the public internet, or an anonymous principal — reaching a resource inside the zone is exactly what Access Analyzer surfaces as a finding.

questions.prompt: A team wants an explicit Deny rule in AWS, the way an Azure NSG can express one, instead of only Allow rules like the Security Group rule above supports. Per Lesson 13, which construct should they reach for?
options: A Network ACL (NACL), attached to the subnet and evaluated in numbered rule order, which supports both explicit Allow and explicit Deny
A second Security Group with a higher priority number set to Deny
A VPC endpoint policy attached to the same security group
A Transit Gateway route table attached to the instance's ENI
questions.explain: A Security Group can only ever Allow — there's no priority field and no explicit Deny, full stop. The real AWS analog to an NSG's explicit Deny is a Network ACL, which attaches to a subnet, evaluates in numbered rule order (lowest number first, first match wins), and supports both explicit Allow and explicit Deny, at the cost of being stateless.

questions.code:
alert tls $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any \
  (tls.sni; content:"update.microsoft.com"; nocase; \
   msg:"allowed update domain"; sid:1000001; rev:1)
questions.prompt: This Suricata-syntax rule is doing FQDN-based filtering. Per Lesson 14, which component is it actually running inside?
options: An AWS Network Firewall stateful rule group
An Azure Firewall Policy application rule collection
An Azure NSG rule
An AWS Security Group rule
questions.explain: AWS Network Firewall does FQDN/domain filtering not through a separate rule type but through a Suricata-syntax stateful rule using the tls.sni or http.host keyword, exactly like this one. Azure Firewall does the same job natively through application rule collections filtering by FQDN directly — a structurally different mechanism, which an NSG or Security Group can't do at all since both filter on IP/port, not domain name.

questions.prompt: Match each private-connectivity term from Lesson 15 to what it actually is.
right: A route table entry routing traffic for S3 or DynamoDB through the endpoint instead of a NAT or internet gateway, with no ENI at all
Azure's NIC with a private IP mapped to one specific PaaS resource instance
AWS PrivateLink's consumer-side ENI, reaching an AWS service or a custom Endpoint Service
Overrides a resource's public FQDN to resolve to its Private Endpoint's private IP instead
questions.explain: A Private Endpoint is Azure's NIC mapped to one PaaS resource instance, made transparent by a Private DNS Zone overriding the public FQDN. AWS's Interface VPC Endpoint is the consumer-side equivalent, an ENI backed by a Network Load Balancer on the provider side. A Gateway Endpoint is structurally different from both — a free, route-table-based mechanism with no ENI, available only for S3 and DynamoDB, with no Azure equivalent.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of forcing spoke-to-spoke traffic through Azure's hub firewall, per Lesson 16, in the correct order.
items: Peer each spoke VNet to the hub VNet
Add a user-defined route on each spoke sending 0.0.0.0/0 (or specific spoke CIDRs) to the firewall's private IP
Traffic from one spoke to another routes through the hub's firewall instead of flowing directly
The firewall's rule collections decide whether to allow or block that cross-spoke traffic
questions.explain: VNet peering alone only connects two VNets directly — it does not automatically route spoke-to-spoke traffic through the hub. Only after peering is combined with user-defined routes sending traffic to the firewall's private IP does cross-spoke traffic actually pass through a central chokepoint, where the firewall's own rules get the final say on whether it's allowed.

questions.prompt: A subscription has dozens of open Defender for Cloud recommendations but zero security alerts. Per Lesson 17, why?
options: No Defender plan is enabled for the resource types involved — Foundational CSPM produces recommendations from configuration assessment alone and never generates an alert on its own
Alerts stay hidden from view until the Secure Score reaches 100%
Recommendations and alerts are simply two different names for the exact same thing
The subscription was never actually connected to Defender for Cloud in the first place
questions.explain: Foundational CSPM is free, always-on, and produces recommendations from point-in-time configuration assessment alone — it never watches runtime behavior and never generates an alert. Alerts only start appearing once a paid Defender plan is enabled for that specific resource type; a resource type with no Defender plan turned on can carry plenty of open recommendations and still never raise an alert.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about AWS Security Hub and GuardDuty, per Lesson 18.
options: Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings from other services into ASFF rather than detecting threats itself
GuardDuty reads CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs without requiring you to deploy an agent
GuardDuty findings flow into Security Hub automatically once both services are enabled in the same account and region
GuardDuty is itself an aggregator, with no built-in threat-detection capability of its own
Security Hub requires installing an agent on every EC2 instance before it can collect any findings
questions.explain: Security Hub's whole value proposition is normalizing findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Access Analyzer, and Config into one consistent ASFF shape — it isn't a detector itself. GuardDuty is the actual detection engine, analyzing existing log sources with no agent required for its core detections, and its findings flow into Security Hub automatically once both are enabled, without you building that integration.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the single highest-leverage control for serverless workload protection, per Lesson 19, isn't a scanning tool at all — it's a tightly scoped, ________-privilege IAM execution role.
questions.explain: A Lambda function with an overly broad execution role turns a minor code vulnerability into full account compromise; a correctly scoped least-privilege execution role limits the blast radius no matter what the function's code does wrong — the highest-leverage serverless control, since there's no OS layer underneath to protect.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the repeatable alert triage sequence from Lesson 20 in the correct order.
items: Read the alert or finding fully, including severity and the MITRE ATT&CK tactic tag
Check whether it's already grouped into a related incident
Establish the resource's blast radius — what identity, network path, and data it actually touches
Rule out a known false-positive pattern using real evidence, not assumption
Decide to contain, monitor, or escalate
Correlate across source-of-truth logs like CloudTrail or Azure Activity Log before closing it out
questions.explain: Triage starts with reading the alert and checking for grouping so you're handling one connected story instead of an isolated tile, then establishes real blast radius before even considering a false-positive explanation — and any false-positive claim has to be backed by evidence, not a guess. Only after that does a contain/monitor/escalate decision get made, and the source-of-truth logs get checked before anything is closed out, so the final record isn't just the alerting tool's own summary.

questions.prompt: A compliance framework requires that the customer retain the ability to independently revoke access to their own data, separate from anything the cloud provider does. Per Lesson 21, which key model actually satisfies this?
options: A customer-managed key (CMK) in Key Vault or KMS, since disabling access to it immediately makes the encrypted data unreadable, even though the ciphertext never moves
A platform-managed key, since it's managed by a team whose only job is managing keys correctly
SSE-S3 default encryption, since every object is still encrypted at rest
Any encryption at rest at all, regardless of which key model is in use
questions.explain: A customer-managed key is the model that gives the customer the 'kill switch' property: revoking access to the key immediately makes the encrypted data unreadable, independent of the cloud provider. A platform-managed key is genuinely secure but gives the customer no independent revocation lever — the key is entirely inside the provider's own infrastructure, which is exactly the capability certain compliance frameworks and contracts require customers to retain.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS access models, per Lesson 22.
options: For a principal to use a KMS key, both their IAM policy and the key's own key policy have to allow it — it's an intersection, not an either/or
Removing the default 'Enable IAM User Permissions' statement from a KMS key's policy can lock everyone out, even with full IAM access
Azure RBAC for Key Vault role assignments show up consistently in access reviews and PIM, unlike the older vault access policy model
AWS KMS stores arbitrary secrets like connection strings and API keys the same way Key Vault does
Rotating a key immediately re-encrypts all data that was previously encrypted under the old key material
questions.explain: A KMS key's own key policy and the caller's IAM policy both have to agree, and most KMS keys delegate control back to IAM through a default statement — remove it and no IAM policy can restore access without the account root user. Azure RBAC for Key Vault is the modern model specifically because it shows up in access reviews and PIM, unlike vault access policies, which are vault-scoped and invisible to those. KMS does not store arbitrary secrets — that's Secrets Manager's job — and rotating a key only changes what's used for new encryption going forward; old ciphertext stays readable via retained key material, it isn't re-encrypted.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: enabling S3 Block Public ________ at the account level overrides any ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access, across every bucket in the account, including future ones.
questions.explain: S3 Block Public Access is deliberately blunt: at the account level it overrides any ACL or bucket policy that would otherwise grant public access, which is why enabling it account-wide is the single highest-leverage control against this entire class of incident, rather than relying on every bucket owner to configure their own bucket correctly.

questions.prompt: Match each data classification term from Lesson 24 to what it actually is.
right: AWS's discovery-based output identifying sensitive content inside S3 objects that were never manually labeled
A label reflecting how much harm a dataset's exposure would cause, such as Public, Internal, Confidential, or Restricted
A classification embedded directly in a file, persisting across downloads, email, and storage moves
The named person or team accountable for deciding and maintaining a dataset's classification
questions.explain: A sensitivity tier is the harm-based label itself; a data owner is who's accountable for assigning and maintaining it. Purview implements classification as a label embedded in the file, persisting wherever it goes. Macie approaches the same problem from the opposite direction — discovery of sensitive content inside objects that were never manually labeled in the first place, since most data landing in S3 arrives through a pipeline, not a person saving a file.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the order an attacker actually follows after obtaining a leaked cloud credential, per Lesson 25's enumerate-escalate-persist-act sequence?
options: Quiet, read-only enumeration first, then an attempt at privilege escalation, then creating a second independent credential to persist, and only then visibly damaging abuse like cryptomining or data exfiltration
Immediate, visibly destructive abuse first, followed by enumeration to figure out what was actually accessible
Persistence first, then enumeration, then escalation, then abuse
Visible abuse always happens before the attacker ever attempts to persist, in every documented real-world case
questions.explain: The documented, consistent pattern starts with quiet, harmless-looking read-only calls like sts:get-caller-identity and list-buckets, moves to privilege-escalation attempts if the identity isn't already privileged, then persistence — a second access key, a new user, an added service principal secret — so rotating the original leaked credential doesn't remove access, and only then does actual damaging abuse happen.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses the entire point of the lesson: an attacker's first calls are almost always quiet and read-only precisely because they look like a harmless script running describe commands, not an obvious smash-and-grab. An organization that only watches for the final, visibly damaging stage is catching this after persistence has already happened.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 26, why does this specific permission combination deserve a documented justification during a policy review?
options: Together, iam:PassRole and ec2:RunInstances let the holder launch an EC2 instance with a far more privileged role attached, then inherit that role's permissions through the instance's metadata service
ec2:RunInstances alone is already equivalent to full administrator access on the account
iam:PassRole by itself lets a principal directly read any S3 bucket in the account
This combination only matters if the principal already holds AdministratorAccess
questions.explain: iam:PassRole plus ec2:RunInstances is one of the catalogued AWS privilege-escalation primitives: the holder launches an EC2 instance, attaches an instance profile tied to a far more privileged role via PassRole, and code running on that instance inherits that role's permissions through the metadata service — not inherently malicious, but exactly the pattern that should raise an eyebrow in a policy review without a documented reason.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about CloudTrail and Azure Activity Log as investigation sources, per Lesson 27.
options: userIdentity.accessKeyId ties an action to the exact credential used, not just the IAM user it belongs to
CloudTrail data events, like S3 object-level GetObject/PutObject, are off by default and must be enabled to prove exactly what was touched
Azure Activity Log, sign-in logs, and audit logs are three separate, complementary log sources, not one combined stream
CloudTrail management events, like AttachUserPolicy and RunInstances, are off by default and must be manually enabled
Azure Activity Log alone fully covers both control-plane operations and sign-in authentication events
questions.explain: accessKeyId lets you trace an action to the exact leaked credential, which matters when a user has multiple keys. Data events are off by default because of volume and cost, while management events are logged by default and cover almost everything in a privilege-escalation sequence. Azure splits investigation across three separate sources — Activity Log for control-plane operations, sign-in logs for authentication, and audit logs for directory changes — and a real investigation pivots across all three rather than treating 'the Azure logs' as one thing.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of containing a compromised AWS credential, per Lesson 28, in the correct order.
items: Preserve forensic evidence, such as snapshotting the affected EBS volume, before touching anything else
Deactivate the specific leaked access key, without deleting it
Apply a deny policy keyed to aws:TokenIssueTime to invalidate sessions already issued from that key
Remediate: rotate credentials and apply a least-privilege policy rewrite
questions.explain: Lesson 28's sequencing is deliberate: evidence first, then containment, then remediation. A security group swap or key deactivation can usually happen immediately without losing evidence, but terminating an instance or deleting credentials before capturing what's needed can't be undone — which is why forensic preservation comes before the containment steps, and remediation comes only after containment holds.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Finworks hardening lab, identity controls (Conditional Access, IAM policy) are hardened before network controls (NSG, Security Group). Per Lesson 29, why?
options: A valid, overly permissive credential walks straight through a locked-down network boundary — a tight NSG or Security Group is not a substitute for tight identity controls
Network controls are technically incapable of being configured before identity controls exist in a tenant
Azure requires NSGs to be configured only after every Conditional Access policy is already in enforced mode
Identity hardening is faster to complete, so it's always scheduled first regardless of risk
questions.explain: The lab's explicit lesson is that an attacker holding a valid, overly permissive credential doesn't need to breach the network boundary at all — they can authenticate and act directly. A tight NSG or Security Group stops network-level access attempts, but it does nothing to stop an attacker who already has working credentials, which is exactly why identity gets hardened first.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Meridian Finworks simulated credential-compromise lab, per Lesson 30.
options: Rotating only the originally leaked secret or key fails to remove the attacker's access, because they added a second credential (addPassword / CreateAccessKey) as a persistence step
Containment — disabling the service principal and deactivating the IAM access keys — happens before the full investigation finishes
The compromise is used as an opportunity to apply the least-privilege rewrite from Lesson 29, not just restore the prior configuration
The lab's remediation deletes the entire app registration to guarantee nothing malicious remains
AWS containment in the lab immediately deletes the compromised IAM user outright
questions.explain: Both halves of the lab show the same persistence pattern — a second credential added after the original leak — which is exactly why rotating only the originally leaked credential doesn't fully remove access. Both halves also contain the credential (disabling sign-in, deactivating keys) before the investigation is fully complete, and both use the incident as the moment to apply least-privilege, not just restore what existed before. Neither half deletes the app registration or the IAM user outright — deleting the app or the user would break legitimate workloads depending on it and destroy evidence.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 31's case study, the Meridian-CICD-Operator role's real danger came from its over-broad ________ — assigned at the subscription level instead of the one resource group the pipeline actually needed — not just its somewhat-too-broad actions.
questions.explain: Two problems compounded each other in the case study, but scope was the more consequential one: a role with somewhat-too-broad actions, assigned tightly at the one resource group it was meant for, would have been a minor finding. The same role assigned subscription-wide meant the service principal could reach every resource group in the subscription — which is why the fix re-scoped the assignment first, before even narrowing the role's actions.
